In 1971, we lived in a town of roughly 50,000 people. In kindergarten and first grade I walked 6 blocks to school every day, and back home at the end of the day. Not once was there fear of being abducted or raped or anything else.

In first grade we learned about the concept of 'negative' numbers in math, and were taught this thing called 'phonics' so we could learn how to read new words... sound it out one syllable at a time. And because our un- diversified student body could speak clear and concise English, once a student sounded out a new word, there was a good chance that the word was at least familiar sounding and therefore easy to understand and comprehend.

Good grades brought rewards (gold stickers and scented markers and your name on the board in colored chalk) and bad behavior was handled with a paddle.

The curriculum was not centered around preparing for a standardized test, it was centered around the State minimum requirements in a few subjects; the rest was focused on basic skills and the local environment/economy. Farming community schools had agricultural classes, schools in heavy manufacturing areas had corporate- funded (corporate assisted is more accurate) shop and drafting and business math classes. When a new hospital was built in town, suddenly the school had a huge grant for biology books and microscopes and such. Schools taught relevant subject matter.

If you couldn't maintain a D- or better, you'd end up in the "L.D." group. Learning Disability, or as we called it "Lotta Dummies."

In the late seventies, the city tried a "joint vocational school" that the poorer schools coulds send their brightest kids to. (White kids in a mostly black areas went to JVS to get the same level of education as the mostly white schools.) Today, that school is just another hangout for the ghetto kids.)

Our little league baseball teams gave out trophies for the good players, and the bad players didn't get to play.

If you sucked at playing an instrument, you didn't get to be in the band. If you couldn't carry a tune, you weren't in the choir. Dumb kids got held back a year.

School was for education, and job applicants with diplomas from certain schools were more likely to get jobs than students with diplomas from other schools.
